label: Verve
rationale: The record that makes the case for Kenny Burrell as an artist rather than a very good guitar player: Creed Taylor put him with Gil Evans, and Evans wrote an orchestra underneath the guitar instead of around it [S2, S3] (obs). Session gravity is the strongest single argument here — the Evans ensemble is Lee Konitz, Steve Lacy, Jimmy Knepper, Jimmy Cleveland, Ron Carter and Elvin Jones, players who define this canon from a dozen other albums, assembled for a guitarist [S1, S3] (obs). Consensus: Wikipedia's review table gives AllMusic 4/5, Record Mirror 4/5, the Penguin Guide 3.5/5, DownBeat 5/5 and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 5/5 [S2] (obs); the album took three 1966 Grammy nominations — Best Instrumental Jazz Performance (Large Group or Soloist with Large Group), Best Album Cover Photography, and Best Arrangement for Evans's 'Greensleeves' [S2] (obs). Defining statement: it is the only Burrell album where a major arranger builds a programme for him, half orchestral, half quintet, with one solo guitar piece — a form never repeated in his catalogue [S1, S2] (inf). Lineage: the Gil Evans orchestral-with-a-soloist model is the same one already in this canon on the Miles Davis records, applied to guitar four years after Sketches of Spain; it is the bridge between Evans's Davis work and the later guitar-with-orchestra tradition [S1, S2] (inf). It still plays: 'Lotus Land' and 'Loie' are immediately legible cold, and 'Downstairs' is an Elvin Jones blues played by a quintet that swings hard [S3] (inf). Not oversold: Penguin sits at 3.5/5, and the album is only sporadically orchestral — the April 1965 quintet tracks are a different, smaller record interleaved with the Evans pieces [S2, S3] (obs).

tracks.title: Last Night When We Were Young

personnel_record.notes: Four sessions. 4 Dec 1964: 'Last Night When We Were Young', 'Moon and Sand'. 15 Dec 1964: 'Lotus Land', 'Loie'. 6 Apr 1965: 'Greensleeves'. 12 Apr 1965: 'Breadwinner', 'Terrace Theme', 'Prelude No. 2', 'Downstairs' (jazzdisco matrix numbers 64VK607-610, 65VK313, 65VK262-264, 65VK327). STUDIO CONFLICT, preserved: jazzdisco and Discogs put all four sessions at Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs; Wikipedia says the two December 1964 sessions were at Webster Hall, New York City. Vinyl Standard publishes both claims side by side without resolving them. The December entries therefore carry epistemic unk rather than picking a winner — only one place row can hang on a session date. Engineer Rudy Van Gelder is named by Wikipedia's production section and by Vinyl Standard; AllMusic serves no credits text for this album (the /credits tab returns the overview page). Instrumental doubles recorded on the primary taxonomy string with the double in notes: Fitzgerald/Marge (English horn), Beckenstein (alto flute, bass clarinet), Tricarico (bassoon, flute), Kamuca (oboe). Four personnel pairs are unresolved 'or' alternates in the sources — trumpet (Coles/Mucci), French horn (Alonge/Watkins), drums (Jones/Persip) — all recorded as unk; do not read them as five-piece horn sections. Gil Evans is arranger and conductor and is deliberately NOT in `personnel`: he plays nothing, and the taxonomy has no value for arranger, so any instrument string would be an invented performance credit. The arrangement credit lives here and in the rationale. Apple: collectionId 1582213328 is the 9-track original programme; the 20-track 'Expanded Edition' is 1442948190.

ballot.case_for: Gil Evans's orchestral settings give Burrell a distinctive showcase beyond the guitar combo, extending the soloist-and-orchestra approach associated with Evans's Miles Davis collaborations without requiring an unproven claim of downstream influence [S1–S3] (inf). The confirmed presence of Lee Konitz, Steve Lacy, Jimmy Knepper, Jimmy Cleveland, and Ron Carter supplies exceptional session gravity [S2, S3] (obs). Ratings reported through Wikipedia—five stars from DownBeat and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide, alongside favorable AllMusic and Penguin assessments—support broad critical recognition, although the original reviews are not supplied [S2] (obs). 'Lotus Land' and 'Loie,' complemented by the combo and solo performances, offer an accessible demonstration of Burrell's expressive range [S1–S3] (inf).
ballot.case_against: The original program combines five orchestral tracks, three quintet performances, and one solo piece; that variety can make it feel like an interrupted Evans collaboration rather than a fully integrated defining statement [S2, S3] (inf). Favorable review scores do not establish recurring canon-list consensus, and the dossier does not substantiate either unique status across Burrell's catalogue or a direct influence on later orchestral guitar records (unk). Unresolved personnel alternates and recording-location conflicts limit the precision of the session-gravity argument, while 'Downstairs' must be credited as an Elvin Jones composition performed with Grady Tate on drums, not evidence of Jones's participation [S2–S4] (obs).
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 judges the distinctive Evans collaboration, broad critical approval, and confirmed personnel sufficient for consensus_core; Reference 2 judges the orchestral/combo discontinuity substantial enough for contested. Both assign strong priority and find no scope boundary; Reference 2's further claims of budget-driven filler and a direct CTI lineage are not established by the dossier.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John give Guitar Forms strong-priority listening consideration, deciding whether its contrasting formats enrich Burrell's statement or weaken its canonical coherence.
